What makes our world? At the largest scales, the realm of stars and galaxies,
its gravitational forces that shapes nature. At the tiniest scales, the realm of
neutrons and protons, its nuclear forces that shapes nature. However, in between
these bookends its electromagnetism the rules.

Electromagnetism is the force that gives us the periodic table, the building
blocks of living things, the sunlight that sustains life, and the colors of a
painting. Our modern lifestyles are based on harnessing the power of
electromagnetism. Even emotions and feelings are ripples of electricity through
our bodies, brains and nerves.

Here we introduce the world of electromagnetism - the building blocks of
chemistry, biology and much more.^-1^ We'll also meet the scientists who
together did for electricity what Newton did for gravity.

Lightning is surely nature's most dazzling showcasing of electricity. Earth's
atmosphere is home to roughly 100 strikes every second, with a typical strike
releasing a billion Joules of energy in a thousandth of a second.^0^ The crack
of thunder that follows the lightning is the shockwave that's caused by air
that's burning and exploding at temperatures times hotter than the sun's
surface. It's no wonder that bolts of lightning can trigger our fight-or-flight
reaction and spook our pets. Our ancestors attributed lightning to supernatural
forces - but today we understand this super natural force is the ubiquitous
electrical force.

The earliest notions of electricity date to 600 BC (a recent event in 200,000
years of human existence). At this time our ancestors had evolved from
hunter-gathers to civilizations with specialized labor - an environment that
facilitated the profession of scholarship. The ancient philosophers considered
questions that ranged from the nature of the universe to the meaning of our
lives. Among their achievements - from breaking free of supernatural believes,
to pursuit of knowledge and understanding - they documented a mysterious new
phenomena involving a material called 'elektron'. Today, we know this material
as amber.

The Greeks discovered that amber, if rubbed with wool or fur, would attract such
lightweight materials as dust, hair, straw and feathers.^1^ This one-of-a-kind
nature of amber seemed quite mysterious and mystical to the Greeks. Indeed it
led some philosophers to attribute a soul or life force to amber in order to
explain its animation of dust, etc. Of course, nowadays this all seems very
California New Agey.

Amber is indeed a remarkable material. Its golden translucence resembles
'bottled' sunshine and through its beauty and rarity it became a prized jewelry
item. The material originates from the resin of the trees of the prehistoric
forests in the dinosaur epoch. Tree resin is the sticky substance that trees
manufacture to repair wounds from broken branches or other damage. But when
entombed and fossilized for tens of millions of years the hardened, polymerized
resin is transformed into amber.

The Greek identification of amber's attractiveness for hair and feathers may
appear rather inconsequential when compared to their achievements in philosophy,
politics, etc. But actually it marks the first step of an astonishing voyage
into the electromagnetic force and the scientific foundations of our
technological age.

It was two thousand years before further progress was made towards understanding
electricity. It was the 'Age of Discovery', the 1500's and 1600's. European
nations were undertaking expeditions across the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian
oceans to the Americas, Asia and Africa. But it was explorations in the homes of
two pensioners that expanded our horizons into the electrical nature of the
material world.

That amber when rubbed can attract a feather was actually just the proverbial
cannery in the coal mine. There's actually nothing special about amber. It
possesses no soul, or life force, or other mumbo-jumbo. At the beginning of the
15th century, William Gilbert - the retired physician to Queen Elizabeth I -
actually discovered that lots of materials can exhibit this property, i.e.,
attracting other light objects when rubbed with wool, fur, etc. Gilbert used the
term "electricity", derived from the Greek "elektron", to name this
attractiveness of rubbed objects.

Gilbert is nowadays considered the discoverer of matter's electric nature and
founder of the electricity's scientific study. He raised our awareness of
"attraction by rubbing" from mysterious amber to pervasive phenomena. Today we
understand that matter is constructed of electrical building blocks and Gilbert
as responsible for exposing this hidden electrical landscape.^2^ Amber wasn't
actually one-of-a-kind.

Today a physicist is either an experimentalist or a theorist. In casual
conversation a theory is often a just a hunch or just a guess. In physics,
however, a theory represents a conceptual foundation and mathematical framework
for understanding nature. A theory explains observations, makes predictions, and
offers both greater clarity and deeper insight. Gilbert was a long-lost
scientist, both an experimentalist and a theorist.

Gilbert proposed an explanation for the electrical attraction of a rubbed body.
He argued the rubbing was responsible for releasing a material he called
effluvium. The effluvium was freed by rubbing into the atmosphere but tethered
and bound to the object. As the effluvium return it pulls inwards the dust,
hair, straw, feathers, etc. Gilbert's idea is rather quaint, It reminds us of
Aladdin rubbing the oil lamp and releasing the Genie or perhaps an effluvium
jack-in-a-box.

One hundred years later, another English pensioner Stephen Gray, further
expanded our electrical horizon. He observed that certain materials could
transport the electrical attractions of rubbed bodies from place to place.
Indeed, first Gray, then others, were able to demonstrate the transportation of
electricity over distances of tens, then hundreds, then thousands of feet using
metal wires (metal wires were new technology in Gray's time).

Gray's finding were truly an instance of a transformative change in a scientific
field - akin to Becquerel's accidental discovery of radioactivity or Fleming's
serendipitous development of penicillin. Today the notion of conductors,
materials that carry electricity, and insulators, materials that don't, is
ingrained in our understanding of the world. From copper wire to silicon
microchips we recognize Gray's findings as the conceptual foundations of our
modern technologies.^3^

The discovery of conductors and insulators was the end of the effluvium as the
source of the attractiveness of a rubbed object. Gray was demonstrating an
"electricity" that was separate from the object that was rubbed. A substance
that slivers through the body of a wire like a serpent. A substance in its own
right, not a possession of a rubbed object. A substance that flows over vast
distance thruogh certain materials.

A new theory of electricity incorporating its flow was clearly needed. At time
there was a theory of heat as a fluid. When heat flowed from hot to cold a fluid
called caloric was flowing from hot to cold. At the tire seemed a new fluid to
add to heat fluid that was an electric fluid.

The next breakthrough was the realization - by French chemist Charles du Fay -
that electricity can actually exhibit both attractive forces and repulsive
forces. Du Fay identified two types of electrical materials - called 'vitreous'
and 'resinous'. He found that like-type materials would repel one another while
unlike-type materials would attract one another. For example, two glass rods
rubbed with silk repel one another, and two plastic rods rubbed with fur repel
one another, but a glass rod and a plastic will attract one another.

In attempting to explain the existence of attraction and repulsion he introduced
This led to ideas of electrical fluids within material bodies which cause the
attraction or repulsion between objects.

Without this feature of electricity both you and I - and the atoms of our bodies
- would cease to exist.

You know Benjamin Franklin as an author and a signer of the US Declaration of
Independence but Franklin was also a scientist and a polymath. You may have
heard the famous story of Franklin flying a kite in thunderstorms to 'collect'
electricity.

which led to notions of positive and negative electric charges.

Franklin explained the existence of two types of electrical materials by
imagining an 'electric fluid' within materials. A substance with fluid-excess
had a positive electric charge (+) and a substance a fluid-deficit had a
negative electric charge (-). When amber is charged by rubbing with fur, some
fluid is transferred between the amber and the fur. Consequently, one material
acquires an excess of fluid (positive charge) and the other material acquires a
corresponding deficit of fluid (negative charge). This language of positive /
negative charges is very handy for expressing the repulsion of like charges, as
both ++ = + and -- = +, and attraction of unlike charges, as both +- = - and -+
= -. Note the fluid is transferred between objects; neither created nor
destroyed.

Nowadays, we understand that Franklin's 'electric fluid' is actually the 'sea'
of negatively charged, electrons within materials. The electric forces between
two objects are the electrical interactions between their electric charges. And
like space is a fundamental dimension of nature, and like time is a fundamental
dimension of nature, electric charge is also fundamental dimension of nature.

It's, however, quite difficult to put into words the meaning of a fundamental
dimensions such as electric charge. In explaining velocity, I can appeal to
everyday experience of things that go fast (rabbits) and things that go slow
(snails). In explaining force, I can appeal to every day experience of a weak
force (a tap on the shoulder) and a strong force (a punch on the nose). I can
also write a equation for velocity in terms of changes in position and intervals
in time and write an equation for force in terms of mass and acceleration in
order to illuminate their physical meanings. In these ways we get a feeling or
picture for what 'velocity' is and what 'force' is.

To define the notion of charge we tend to simply list its known features.
Electric charge is an intrinsic property of a particle (e.g. electron, proton)
or an object (e.g. glass, amber) that is responsible for the electric forces
between all charged objects. There are two types of electric charge; we denote
them positive and negative. Electric charge is conserved; we cannot create it
and we cannot destroy it.^2^ And electric charge is quantized; all protons
carrying a charge of +1.6x10^-19^ Coulombs and all electrons carrying a charge
of -1.6x10^-19^ Coulombs. Through such properties of charge as its conservation
and its quantization we get to know it.

That matter's made of charged constituents is key to explaining both electrical
charging of materials and electrical currents in materials. Over the duration of
this course, we'll discover that electric charge is actually the root of
electricity, magnetism and light and also the heart of atoms, molecules, living
things and modern technology. But why charge actually exists, why charge has two
types, why charge is conserved, and why charge is quantized, are still mysteries
to today's scientists.

A celebrated example of charging by rubbing is the Millikan oil drop experiment.
Robert Millikan was a famous American scientist who received the 1928, Physics
Nobel Prize. In the experiment he suspended minuscule, charged, water droplets
by means of the earth's gravitational force and an applied electrical force. The
procedure permitted the measurement of the charge of the droplets and revealed
the charges were always in integer multiplies of 1.6x10^-19^C. His remarkable
experiment had observed droplets with one, two, three, ... excess electrons and
thereby determined the basic unit of electrical charge.

Another spectacular example of charging by rubbing is thunder clouds.
Thunderclouds are battle grounds between warm rising air and cold falling air.
Within the warm up-draft are vast numbers of tiny water droplets and within the
cold down-draft are likewise vast numbers of tiny ice crystals. Collisions
between droplets and crystals causes charging through the different proclivities
of warm water and cold ice for gaining or losing an electrons.
Collision-by-collision this mechanism builds regions of cloud with massive
quantities of excess-negative charge and excess-positive charge. And then
there's thunder and lightning.
